# MRI Safety

{{< include "includes/WIP-callout.qmd" >}}

## Safety Considerations Overview

This chapter covers four topics:

* Ferromagnetic hazards and projectile risks
* Magnet quenching and helium venting systems
* Field strength safety limits
* Real-world accidents

<!-- Note: safety-quench-description.png in images/ch04/ is unused, but deliberately so — it is the other build step of the MR Quench slide already shown below. -->

## Main Magnetic Field (B0): General Properties

![B0 field properties relevant to safety: field strengths used clinically, field uniformity specifications, and field stability.](images/ch04/safety-b0-properties.png){#fig-safety-b0-properties fig-alt="Slide listing B0 safety properties: human body-size scanners at 1.5T, 3T, and a few at 9.4T; uniformity of 5 ppm over 50 cm; stability of 0.1 ppm/hour; and use of small bore magnets for animal and chemical experiments."}

Human body-size MR scanners are most commonly operated at 1.5 T and 3 T, with a small number at 7 T and very few at 9.4 T or above. Field uniformity is typically 5 parts per million (ppm) over a 50 cm diameter spherical volume. Field stability is maintained at better than 0.1 ppm/hour (less than 1000 ppm/year). MR physicists also use small-bore systems at much higher field strengths for animal imaging and for chemical spectroscopy; a small bore makes both the high field and the necessary homogeneity easier to achieve.

## Ferromagnetic Objects and Projectile Hazards

![Ferromagnetic objects near MR scanners become dangerous projectiles: examples include a chair, oxygen canister, and power supply drawn into the bore.](images/ch04/safety-ferromagnetic-projectiles.png){#fig-safety-ferromagnetic-projectiles fig-alt="Four-panel figure showing a chair, oxygen canister, and power supply that have been drawn into MRI scanner bores by the static magnetic field. From Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e."}

The primary physical danger of working around an MRI magnet is the **projectile effect**: ferromagnetic objects experience a strong attractive force toward the magnet bore that increases rapidly as the object approaches. Common hazardous objects include oxygen canisters, IV poles, tools, scissors, and any item containing iron or steel. The magnet is always on, which is what makes this hazard so persistent: it does not switch off between scans, or overnight, or when the scanner is idle.

The field itself is a different matter. There is no known biological mechanism by which the **static** $B_0$ field damages tissue at the field strengths currently in use. Subjects moving quickly through a strong field do sometimes report transient effects — dizziness, a metallic taste, or visual flickers — which subside when they stop moving. Rapidly **switching** gradient fields can induce peripheral nerve stimulation, and RF power deposition is limited by SAR, which is why coil designs are simulated for safety (@sec-rf-coils-overview).

## Real-World Safety Incidents

### Local Example: Mountain View

![News report of a projectile accident at a Mountain View MRI facility.](images/ch04/safety-local-accident.png){#fig-safety-local-accident fig-alt="Screenshot of a KTVU news article headlined 'Freak accident in Mountain View exposes MRI safety flaws', with a photo of the MRI room after an incident."}

## Magnet Quench

![Sequence of photographs showing a superconducting magnet quench event at a manufacturing facility.](images/ch04/safety-quench-sequence.png){#fig-safety-quench-sequence fig-alt="Six-panel time sequence showing a magnet quench, with helium vapor erupting from the scanner in a large white cloud."}

A superconducting magnet requires no ongoing electrical power once charged — the current flows indefinitely as long as the wire remains below its critical temperature. If the cooling system fails, the wire warms, develops resistance, generates heat, which drives further warming in a runaway process. The liquid helium rapidly converts to gas (expanding by a factor of ~700), pressure builds, and the system releases the helium through a dedicated vent pipe in an event called a **quench**.

In an open space a quench is spectacular but not immediately dangerous. In an enclosed room, the escaping helium — which is inert — can displace oxygen and create an asphyxiation hazard. MRI scanner rooms are required to have helium venting systems for this reason.

[Here are links to many YouTube videos of quenches, and tutorials about an MR Quench.](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=Controlled+MRI+Magnet+Quench)

## Hitachi Open-Platform Scanner

![Hitachi 0.7T open-platform surgical MRI scanner — an alternative geometry that reduces some access constraints.](images/ch04/safety-hitachi-open-scanner.png){#fig-safety-hitachi-open-scanner fig-alt="Photo of a Hitachi 0.7T open-platform MRI scanner with a horizontal gap between the upper and lower magnet poles, allowing lateral access to the patient."}

Open-platform scanners use a vertical field geometry with a gap between the upper and lower magnet assemblies. The lower field strength (typically 0.7T or below) limits SNR compared to closed-bore systems, but the open geometry allows surgical access and is better tolerated by claustrophobic patients.

The forces involved near a high-field magnet are difficult to appreciate without direct experience. The force on a ferromagnetic object depends on both the field strength and how fast the field is changing with position, so it grows very steeply as the object approaches the bore entrance — an object that feels merely heavy a few feet away can be torn out of your hands at the bore. Even experienced MRI staff must maintain strict protocols to prevent accidents.
